title: GUDA: Counterfactual Group-wise Training Data Attribution for Diffusion Models via Unlearning
claim: Instead of expensively retraining a model per group, approximate each counterfactual by unlearning from one shared full model, then score it against the retraining gold standard.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right; gray expensive retraining branch stacked above pink efficient branch
description: Three rounded panels read left to right. The left panel, 'Data & Groups', shows the training set D split into groups D1 to DN. Group D_k is highlighted in red as the target for removal, with sample art images beneath each group. The middle panel, 'Counterfactual Model Construction', feeds a central Full Model (θ^full) into two stacked branches. The top gray branch retrains without group k to get the LOGO model, labeled 'Expensive'. The bottom pink branch fine-tunes to remove group k to get the Unlearned Model, labeled 'Efficient' and 'GUDA'. The right panel, 'Attribution Scoring & Evaluation', shows a generated dog image. Two bar charts for LOGOA_k and GUDA_k sit beside ELBO-difference formula boxes. They feed a 'Fidelity to LOGOA (Evaluation)' box, with 'Goal: High Fidelity to LOGOA' in red text. Gray versus pink coding carries the contrast.
caption: Overview of the \method\ (\methodfull) framework. Instead of retraining $N+1$ models from scratch (LOGO), \method\ starts from the all-group model $\theta^{\mathrm{full}}$ and applies machine unlearning to obtain approximate counterfactual models $\theta^{\mathrm{ul}}_{-k}$ for each group $k$. Attribution is computed by comparing the ELBO of generated samples under the all-group model versus each unlearned model, providing an efficient approximation to the counterfactual target validated against LOGO.
abstract: Training-data attribution for vision generative models aims to identify which training data influenced a given output. While most methods score individual examples, practitioners often need group-level answers (e.g., artistic styles or object classes). Group-wise attribution is counterfactual: how would a model's behavior on a generated sample change if a group were absent from training? A natural realization of this counterfactual is Leave-One-Group-Out (LOGO) retraining, which retrains the model with each group removed; however, it becomes computationally prohibitive as the number of groups grows. We propose GUDA (Group Unlearning-based Data Attribution) for diffusion models, which approximates each counterfactual model by applying machine unlearning to a shared full-data model instead of training from scratch. GUDA quantifies group influence using differences in a likelihood-based scoring rule (ELBO) between the full model and each unlearned counterfactual. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and artistic style attribution with Stable Diffusion show that GUDA identifies primary contributing groups more reliably than semantic similarity, gradient-based attribution, and instance-level unlearning approaches, while achieving ~100x speedup on CIFAR-10 over LOGO retraining.
